item.title: How I'm thinking about different types of automated alignment
item.description:
I used to think of "automating alignment" as a natural category. But when I tried to think through the strategic implications, I realised that it depends a lot on the type of work. I'm now thinking of it in three buckets:

  1. Empirical alignment research: design and execution of alignment-relevant experiments (for a given notion of what we’re aiming for)
  2. Conceptual alignment research: theoretical or judgement-driven work to improve our understanding of what we’re aiming for and how to achieve it (including how to measure it)
  3. Direct alignment work: making particular AI systems more aligned (including via inputs such as training data)

In the rest of this post I'll walk through my current takes on these in terms what’s needed for automation, how good or bad they look, what our priorities might be (to the extent we're interested in automating alignment[1]), etc.

Automating empirical alignment research

This is the most obvious fit for the AI capabilities we’re getting at the moment. You want to know more about the relationship between some alignment-relevant variables? Great, an AI agent can design and run that experiment for you. You want to know what training methods help your alignment benchmark go up? In the not-too-distant future, AI agents will probably be able to do this too. When we have the automated capabilities researchers we seem on track for, this is exactly the kind of thing they’ll likely be able to do a lot of.

Note that I’m not counting the design of benchmarks/metrics/evals as part of this bucket. In current practice that’s tightly intertwined with empirical alignment research, and often the hardest part of it. But for automation purposes it clusters much more with conceptual work; it’s easy to imagine automating the rest of empirical research without it (as AI capabilities generally get automated); and I think its automation has different strategic upshots.

The capabilities that are needed for automating empirical alignment research very heavily overlap with the capabilities needed for automating AI capabilities research. Therefore, it doesn’t seem like a priority to try to accelerate this type of automation.

However, the prospect of getting a lot of automated empirical alignment work before we have good versions of other types of automated alignment work increases the priority of work which complements it. Significantly, that may mean better specification of the kind of numbers we would like measured/targeted.

Automating conceptual alignment research

What about automating the type of metric choice/construction that we’ve just said would be a good complement to automating empirical alignment work? Or more generally improving our understanding of how to think about alignment, what we’re even aiming for, etc.?

This is essentially theoretical research. Automating it is trickier than automating empirical work because of the lack of verifiable signal about what constitutes progress.

Accelerating the automation of conceptual research is somewhat fraught (feeding into some dangerous technologies), but seems helpful for a number of high-priority areas, including macrostrategy as well as conceptual alignment work. Overall it seems likely good to do, if we can.

Methods for helping to automate conceptual research broadly might include:

  • Curating training data for finetuning
  • Building scaffolds to try to elicit more research progress from current or future models
  • Building methods to extract more signal from existing conceptual research data
  • Building benchmarks for conceptual research capabilities, that can be targeted by AI researchers (or potentially by automated capabilities researchers)
    • Or just identifying good ideas for benchmarks, even if they aren’t fully implemented

Automating direct alignment work

As well as learning more about what it takes to make systems more aligned, sometimes we want to just make our actual systems as aligned as possible.

This overlaps with empirical alignment work, but the emphasis is different:

  • Empirical alignment work is science
  • Direct alignment work is engineering

Automating direct alignment work could include a lot of activities which leverage scalable cognition for alignment-relevant purposes. This could include careful auditing of particular RL environments or training data, or direct monitoring/supervision of systems during training. RLAIF for alignment properties is a form of automated direct alignment work; Claude 3 Opus’s apparent self-alignment was another (albeit accidental in that case; but if we knew how to reproduce or generalize the behaviour perhaps it could happen deliberately).

I think that the limit of automating direct alignment work would be a form of system 2 learning, where updates are not made blindly towards a training objective, but reflectively by an AI system that was already sufficiently aligned (not necessarily having robustly good values already — just enough genuine care about being aligned, and honesty with itself, that its reflective updates tend to move it further in that direction), and wished to become more so — whatever the deep true version of aligned should mean[2]. Embarking on such a path could be fraught (because of difficulty in being confident that the starting conditions were in the right basin of attraction), but compared to other alignment approaches, it has the benefit that it might leverage the full strength of the AI’s cognition to help, so that its “self-improvement” in an alignment direction is a closer analogue to meditation than to self-performed neurosurgery.

So, accelerating the automation of direct alignment work could include:

  • Designing (and analysing) setups that can deploy AI labour to help with direct alignment work
  • Designing paradigms (that could then be tested empirically) that allow AI to be a more active participant in its own alignment
  • Producing data (or scaffolds) to help improve AI taste at the alignment-relevant tasks necessary for this

Interactions

These categories blur and interact in a number of different ways:

  • Automated direct alignment techniques may be good subjects for empirical experiments
    • This is not completely reliant on having good metrics for alignment; developing a science of what’s going on with different attempts at automated direct alignment could be useful even if we don’t yet know what “good” looks like
    • Automated hill-climbing might get you to very strong direct alignment approaches — but this does rely on having good enough metrics
      • i.e. we could plausibly be in a regime where we’re better at reasoning about and implementing training setups that in fact lead to aligned systems than we are at accurately measuring their alignment. In that case, optimising for our best alignment metrics might produce worse alignment outcomes than following our best-guess direct alignment process.
  • If you can do a good job of automating conceptual alignment research, you should be approximately done (“winning” on the alignment challenge)
    • Since that should then be able to do the relevant parts of prep for automating the other types of alignment work, and being appropriately confident in your techniques for them
  • You could also in principle do a good enough job at direct alignment that the systems you’re building are entirely safe
    • But I think it will be hard to have very strong confidence in that before improving our automation of the conceptual side; and so each new generation of AI might pose a challenge — will your alignment techniques transfer, or will your luck run out?
  • So: the main goal (from an existential risk perspective) for automating empirical research and direct alignment work is to get our systems safe enough to robustly avoid catastrophe (“not losing”) for long enough that we can automate conceptual alignment research to a very high quality level
  • There will likely be approaches that allow you to leverage automation of empirical research to get better automation of conceptual work
    • e.g. Taking Talkie or another LLM with only vintage training data, and working out how to get it to perform well at rederiving more modern theoretical work

Priorities

Two major uncertainties that affect priorities:

  1. How much loss-of-control risk is early?
    • If there’s a bunch, then putting more energy into the “not losing” part of things makes sense
    • If the main misalignment risk comes when we’re getting systems that can perform well even on tasks without verifiable rewards (like long-term strategy to allow them to plot sophisticated power-seeking campaigns), then it makes sense to put more energy into accelerating the “winning” part, and so perhaps move it earlier in time so that it comes before some crucial challenge that we otherwise wouldn’t be able to face
      • Note that in this world, the win state and the biggest threats rely on capabilities that from our vantage point look quite similar — in that they require high-quality thinking about novel situations without verifiable rewards — so it’s quite plausible that even a modest acceleration could change the sequencing
  2. How close might we be to decent automated conceptual alignment work, if we approach it relatively directly?
    • If it’s not hideously out of reach, then it looks more like the kind of thing where human intervention to speed it up (by building benchmarks and scaffolds, and curating data) could make the difference
    • If so, the full suite of activities mentioned above as precursors for conceptual alignment work looks helpful
    • If automated conceptual research is too hard, maybe the direct interventions don’t actually do much — in this world, automated conceptual research falls out of stronger AI driving automated (empirical) research programs to work out how to automate conceptual research
      • So trying to target conceptual alignment work directly might be obsoleted as a way to accelerate the “winning” moment, and it’s a higher priority to get things safe enough that we robustly don’t lose through the period where the automated capabilities research is speeding up
      • I’d note that building metrics/benchmarks for conceptual research, that can be targeted by later automated empirical work, looks more robust to this concern than other forms of targeting automated conceptual research

My personal guesses on these uncertainties are that most of the loss-of-control risk comes later (after AI is superhuman even at tasks that don’t have verifiable rewards), and that it is possible to directly approach decent automated conceptual research. However, mostly I’m pretty uncertain — which argues in favour of hedging by investing some in all of the paths.

  1. ^

    I'm not saying "I think automated alignment is the best plan" (I currently don't; I'm more excited by epistemic and coordination uplift enabling robust coordination). But I think (1) it's a backstop to other plans and might work so is worth some investment, and (2) in any case it's helpful for assessing what we think of automated alignment to have a better sense of what it even means.

  2. ^

    So the system would need something like the type of understanding that conceptual alignment research is aiming at. But conceptual research aims to understand things abstractly; the understanding which such a system had might be more akin to a lived experience and understanding. I say this without taking any stance on whether such AI systems would have conscious experience; it does rely on something like introspective ability, but that’s something we’ve seen (to some extent) in LLMs today.

item.title: Delaying Internal Deployments Until After X Days of Safety Testing
item.description:
This post reflects my own takes, and not that of my employer's.

This is a simple idea: before a new model can be deployed internally, you must first test it for a minimum, fixed period.

You can adjust various axes of this proposal:

  1. Duration of the wait: in calendar time, or until you fulfill some condition.
  2. What it blocks: external deployment, internal deployment, or the training of future checkpoints.
  3. When the fixed period starts: from the first checkpoint, the final checkpoint, or any checkpoint that is “sufficiently similar / representative” to the one that is ultimately deployed.

One concrete target that I like is: “No checkpoint may be used internally for purposes beyond safety testing, until at least X calendar days after its hash is filed with an auditor.”

This is one specific implementation of internal deployment lags, an idea that the AI Futures Project (AIFP) briefly discusses in How to pace the US frontier as “AI R&D can only be conducted or assisted by AIs that were trained at least 9 months ago”.

What does this look like when implemented?

Let’s run through a scenario to pin down the details of this proposal. The places where it could go wrong are in the open questions at the end.

  • A legislative body sets a minimum waiting period of X calendar days (starting at 10 and possibly ratcheting up to 90). No checkpoint in a covered model family may be used internally, beyond safety testing, until X calendar days after its hash is filed with an auditor. Continuing to train a checkpoint’s own weights does not count as internal use.
    • The alternative is for the wait to also block the training of checkpoint N+1, and not just the internal use of checkpoint N. I didn’t go with this because it incentivizes developers to pull out fewer checkpoints for testing, and because delaying training results in an algorithmic overhang.
  • More capable models start exhibiting problems that are harder to surface in short periods (e.g. swarms, long-horizon, memory), so X should possibly increase over time.
  • A model family becomes covered as soon as any of its checkpoints (pre-, mid- or post-trained) is substantially more capable than the last model to complete its wait. If the developer initially claims that the model is not covered but later finds that it is, they will be subject to some penalty (to be determined). There is also an absolute floor on capabilities, so that this doesn’t apply to lots of benign models.
  • In an emergency, the auditor can authorize one named checkpoint to be used early, only for responding to a specific incident (e.g. a harmful model is already causing damage, and the developer has just trained a patched model that could counter it). The standards/legislative body confirms or revokes this within [X days].
  • The developer continually pulls checkpoints throughout the training process. They first send an auditor a hash, a short fingerprint of the exact weights; then, they carry out safety testing for X days before deploying a checkpoint broadly internally without the below rules. All work has to be fully transparent to auditors.
  • Options for how the X days are structured:
    • Staged testing
      • Stage 1, first part of X: pre-registered evals and named testers in an isolated environment.
      • Stage 2, second part of X: broad monitored internal use, but the model can’t launch jobs, merge code, write to training data, or touch prod.
    • Parallel, hidden runs: whenever someone at the developer uses a cleared model, the new checkpoint gets the same task in a separate sandboxed copy of the environment. Its outputs go only to monitors and the safety team, never back to the person who asked.

Open questions

The rule itself

  • Should we also allow capability testing? What about ML R&D tasks? One way to game this is to register thousands of tasks from your open R&D backlog, and call running them a capability eval. The outputs are real research (e.g. a faster kernel), and even if you ban using them, people still have to read the transcripts to grade them, so they learn what worked. Pre-registering evals doesn’t help, since it fixes the task list in advance but doesn’t check whether the tasks are live problems. You might end up needing a compute cap.
  • Should we give exemptions for doing safety research? This is an important crux to ask alignment researchers about. Without an exemption, safety research is done with a model that is X days behind, but a blanket exemption lets capabilities work pose as safety work.
  • Should a safety fix (e.g. more post-training, or redoing RL from an earlier checkpoint) restart the X-day wait? It would be bad if it did, as Avi Brach-Neufeld points out here. A developer that finds an issue on day 8 of testing loses more time than one that finds it on day 2, so the rule penalizes finding and fixing problems during the wait. This is probably tolerable at small X, but gets worse as X increases. If safety fixes don’t restart the clock, however, developers could just call capabilities training “safety”.
  • What is the principle behind how much X increases?
  • How large is the risk that an emergency clause would be abused?
  • Concerning behaviours aren’t necessarily caught during pre-deployment testing windows, and are often caught through subsequent monitored internal use. How much are we willing to trade off the value of catching some misaligned behaviours via monitoring internal deployments, vs. being able to pace internal R&D?

Which models are covered

  • How is “substantially more capable” defined: effective compute, or something like the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI)?
  • How would an auditor check that the developer has faithfully stuck to the “more capable” definition?
  • How do you avoid bringing classifiers built using a frontier model into scope?
  • Can a developer keep using earlier checkpoints from a family after it becomes covered?
  • A developer could train a second model family and keep it just under the “substantially more capable” line, so it’s never covered. Researchers could then use that family right away, while use of the main family is on hold. This only gets them so far, since coverage is measured against the last model to complete its wait, and an uncovered family never completes one, so the second family can only be ahead by the “substantially more capable” margin. This becomes a bigger problem if the capability measure itself can be gamed.

Gaming the wait

  • How can we stop a developer from using a checkpoint for acceleratory AI R&D work during the wait, by labeling that work as an allowed activity (i.e. any AI R&D task whose output gets used for anything other than testing that checkpoint)?
    • How can we cleanly separate out safety testing from other activities?
    • A developer could give a new model a real task during training, such as writing faster training code, and then use that code to train other models before the new model has completed the X-day wait.
    • A developer could make every researcher an A/B tester, so that they use the new model for normal work and rate its answers, and the developer calls this training. Similarly, a developer could have an RL environment that is just how well the model does actual work inside the company.
  • In stage 1 of staged testing, you run the risk that named testers run large agent swarms for capabilities work, in which case the only difference is that there are fewer humans in the loop. This is probably somewhat mitigated by pre-registering evals, but it’s difficult to still allow AWT.
  • In stage 2, you can still copy paste model outputs into training data, or into code and research plans. A developer could also store outputs from the wait and use them the day the checkpoint clears, without breaking any rule. Should there be a blanket ban on training on outputs from the wait, and how would anyone check?
  • In stage 2, how will you detect if the model is launching jobs, merging code, writing to training data, or touching prod?
  • Developers can game the wait by making lots of models and testing all of them at once, so that the testing period ends up being an AI R&D period. For example, with a 30-day wait, a developer could pull out a checkpoint every day and “test” them all, so that researchers always have a day-old model. Possible mitigations are to cap the number of checkpoints that can be tested concurrently, cap total compute across the entire testing period, or pre-register the kind of testing you want to do during the period.
  • If each developer could write its own definition of “safety testing”, a developer could call any monitored employee use testing and move faster. Others would then face pressure to do the same, until the rule no longer binds anyone. A shared template would help, but it depends on the auditor being competent and independent.

Parallel, hidden runs

  • There’s no human interacting with the new model, so you miss problems that only show up in back-and-forth with a person. A situationally aware model might also notice it’s in a sandbox and behave differently. Is this okay?
  • How big of a problem is leak risk from reviewers back to capabilities researchers?

Verification

  • How can you mitigate the risk that the developer simply does not send the hash of a given checkpoint to the auditor? Potentially:
    • In the near term: the auditor spot-checks that the weights running on internal endpoints match filed hashes. One complication is that a hash of the exact weights changes with any conversion (e.g. quantization, sharding, or a change of number format), so the weights being served would often not match the filed checkpoint byte for byte. You would need either a standard way of serializing the weights, or a hash of the version that is actually served.
    • In the longer run: hardware attestation.

Could this be used as a speed dial?

The wait gives developers and auditors more time for safety testing. X could also be used as a speed dial, which a standards/legislative body could turn up or down if it wanted to modulate the pace of AI progress.

I think that this only works as a speed dial if this proposal delays internal R&D loops; delaying external deployment would mainly have second order effects like:

  • Each launch shifts the start of new revenue back by a short period. These delays don’t stack across launches, since every launch is shifted back by the same amount. This could still in principle strain a given developer’s ability to pay for compute contracts, but the impact might be small, since I expect that you are mostly shifting when new revenue starts instead of losing it entirely.
  • Some reduction of race dynamics, though I expect the effect size to be quite small.

It’s unclear whether this causes a one-time delay in when the most capable model can be used internally, or a lasting change in the pace of AI progress. This depends on how much the newest model speeds up R&D compared with a model that’s X days older. I have a hunch that, if implemented well, this proposal would have a larger impact on the pace of recursive self-improvement (RSI) itself than on the onset of RSI.

Much of the value of this proposal will depend on how effectively you can specify what counts as “safety testing”, given that the most useful safety testing often looks like real use. A narrower definition limits how much acceleratory AI R&D work gets through during the wait, but it cuts against giving safety researchers signal of misalignment that only show up in broad, realistic use.

What are the benefits and drawbacks of this proposal?

Benefits include:

  • As a speed dial, this should get stronger as things speed up, as the gap between the newest model and the last cleared model gets bigger, whereas a compute cap might stop binding if most of the progress is coming from algorithms.
  • Developers would be incentivized to hand the checkpoint to an auditor as soon as possible so that they can deploy more quickly (assuming that they can’t use unfiled checkpoints without being detected).
  • It doesn’t result in an algorithmic overhang, because you still allow training, and presumably any new compute multipliers you find are put into the newest model that you are training.
    • The exception is if a developer can secretly stock up capabilities outputs during the wait, e.g. by storing work from hidden parallel runs or ML R&D evals.

Drawbacks include:

  • Developers get a lot of signal on misalignment by internally deploying a model. You don’t get less misalignment signal for a given model, since it will be broadly deployed eventually, but you delay the timeline on which a safety issue can be fixed. Today a problem seen in real use can feed into the next model’s training almost straight away; under this proposal, a model will get X more days of training before an issue is detected.
    • Mitigations: the parallel hidden runs idea; a norm that when real use of the cleared model turns up a problem, you test all the waiting checkpoints for it straight away.
  • Safety research done with the model is X days behind.
  • Unlike proposals that limit the most capable model you have at a given time (like compute caps), this limits the most capable model you can use. The risk incurred by foreign competitors stealing model weights is therefore comparatively higher.
  • It’s hard to verify how a checkpoint was used, so you may rely very heavily on auditor judgement.
  • This proposal may not work with continual learning, if there were a breakthrough.


Discuss

item.title: Q3.5 Timelines Update: Looks Like the Intelligence Explosion Will Happen in 2027 After All
item.description:
We want to get this post out quickly given the urgency of the topic. It’s possible that there are some errors in the modeling, but we think it’s very unlikely that they undermine the high level conclusions. We would love to be corrected on any mistakes we made.

METR recently estimated that Anthropic is now making AI progress about twice as fast as its historical rate (they would not be surprised by anything from 1.3x to 3x), and guessed that “perhaps ≈80%” of the current acceleration is due to AI. If they’re right, that implies an AI-driven acceleration that is 5 months ahead of the AI 2027 scenario.

This level of acceleration due to AI is very unexpected. Previously, Daniel, the most bullish of us, assigned a 50% chance of Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR)[1] before 2029. SAR is roughly the point at which a company would rather fire all their human researchers and rely solely on automated AI researchers than have a team of the best human researchers in the world with no AIs.[2]

Now, all of us forecast that Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will likely arrive at some point in 2027 (assuming no substantial deliberate slowdown).[3]We also predict a 35-65% chance that Top-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI), AIs that can automate all white-collar work, will arrive before 2028. While there were many factors and sources of evidence that influenced us, the single biggest source was the METR report.[4].

If SAR is coming in 2027, it is incredibly urgent to pause or substantially ‘pace’ frontier AI development, with the ideal being an industry-wide pause followed by an international agreement. Companies are not on track to align a SAR, and using a misaligned SAR to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) will put us in an extremely bad position. Additionally, if we train SAR in the near future, China will probably be able to steal the training recipe and maybe even the model weights (more).[5]

Timelines/Takeoff Update Summary

We estimate that METR’s report implies a 1.7x AI-attributable acceleration in the pace of progress today, relative to historical levels. This surprises our model; we made our most recent timelines forecasts less than three months ago, and even the most aggressive model-based distribution (Daniel’s) assigned less than 4% to the pace of progress being sped up by at least 1.7x in November 2026.[6] 1.7x AI-attributable acceleration is a bigger deal than it may seem; e.g., it’s a much bigger deal than making employees 1.7x more productive.

We focus in this post primarily on forecasting when Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will arrive. We also discuss Top-Expert-Dominating-AI (TED-AI): AIs that are better than top human experts at virtually all tasks. (more)

In this post, we forecast SAR and TED-AI using the following approaches:

Simple models:

  • Research taste linear extrapolation: Even assuming that the recent pace of progress doesn’t accelerate further due to automation, the fact that the recent trend is above historical rates is a big update to our timelines; a linear extrapolation of the recent rate of AI progress predicts that SAR will likely be achieved by the end of 2027.
  • Labor uplift extrapolation: An exponential extrapolation of self-reported labor uplift predicts SAR in mid-2028. In addition to not modeling automation, there are reasons to think that an exponential is too conservative. However, self-reports may be too bullish.
  • Extrapolating Anthropic automation levels: Anthropic recently shared a graph showing how the percentage of R&D tasks at various automation levels has changed over time. Extrapolating this predicts SAR in late 2027; this method also doesn’t model speedup from automation.
  • Extrapolating software R&D uplift per unit of ECI: AI software R&D uplift must have recently been increasing by a larger factor with each ECI point. If we linearly extrapolate the rate at which this “factor of extra uplift per ECI point” is increasing, we get SAR in Dec 2027 (if we assume that the self-reported AI labor uplift chart is accurate) or July 2027 (if we assume that there was no meaningful automation 12 months ago and all the speed-up has happened after then).
  • Tom Davidson’s toy model: Predicts superintelligence in around a year conditional on a software-only singularity, so SAR sometime in 2027.

Filtered AI Futures Model (AIFM): Keeping the existing AIFM (including parameter distributions), and filtering for trajectories that match METR’s AI-attributable pace of progress acceleration estimates. This serves 2 purposes on top of the simple extrapolations:

  1. Modeling how automation changes the rate of progress, allowing forecasting reasonably beyond SAR.
  2. Informing what parameter settings in the simple research taste extrapolation are plausible.

The results of these methods:

How to think about these results:

  • The simple research taste extrapolation, which is a simplified version of the AIFM, gives July or September 2027, depending on whether you account for parameter uncertainty. Other simple models predict late 2027 to mid-2028.
  • When conditioned on 1.7x Nov 2026 AI-attributed acceleration, the AIFM predicts a SAR median of Feb 2027. This is faster than the simple research taste extrapolation because it usually has a higher level of Sep 2026 research taste (in the median case, matching a median researcher),[7] and it accounts for further automation.
  • When additionally conditioning on a 1.2x May 2026 AI-attributed acceleration, predictions get slower because it indicates a lower rate of growth than is typical when only conditioning on 1.7x in Nov.

We then explore hypotheses for why the AI Futures Model was wrong, including parameter adjustments and modeling changes. The analysis is highly preliminary, and we were unable to come to strong conclusions. Our top candidates for what explains where we went wrong are:

  • Near-AC coding skills result in more AI R&D uplift than we anticipated. This could explain the combination of ~1.7x AI-attributable acceleration in Nov and (very roughly) ~1.2x in May, without AIs already having high enough research taste to contribute to the acceleration. In this case, the gradual acceleration no longer implies a low research taste slope, so steeper slopes and faster taste-driven takeoffs are more likely.
  • Skills besides coding and research taste (the two included in the AIFM), e.g., data generation, are driving acceleration. This potentially would have similar implications to the above bullet. But it’s unclear.
  • Conversion of uplift to pace of progress is too conservative. I.e., we modeled diminishing returns to AI research effort too harshly. This would point toward a faster takeoff.

Here’s an example trajectory from the AIFM showing how things might go if the cause of our prediction error was underestimating AI R&D uplift from near-AC coding skills:[8]

After discussing some other considerations, we share our all-things-considered forecasts (conditional on AGI projects/companies not slowing down):

Note that the gap between a person’s SAR median and TED-AI median is not their median time from SAR to TED-AI. Because the distributions of the time until SAR and of the time from SAR to TED-AI both have long right tails, the difference of the medians is typically larger than the median of the difference, so subtracting the two columns tends to overstate the median time between the two milestones.

METR’s estimates imply that progress is currently sped up by 1.7x due to AI

In METR’s recent assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic, they estimate that, over the past year, AI R&D progress has accelerated by ~2x relative to the trend before Oct 2025. METR estimates that ~80% of current acceleration is downstream of AI (as opposed to other factors), which implies a 1.7x acceleration due to AI (1.67–1.74x depending on how the 80% is read; see appendix).[9]

Both of these estimates rely significantly on evidence METR wasn’t able to share: METR says that “Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions”, which makes it difficult to know exactly what the 2x and 80% estimates are based on.

The 2x acceleration figure is partially based on evidence METR was allowed to share: the following graph, depicting benchmark scores recently growing at roughly twice the historical rate. The 80%/1.7x estimates have no comparable public support.

This estimate is produced by fitting trendlines to the performance of models as judged by AECI, Anthropic’s internal version of Epoch’s Capabilities Index (ECI). The trend fitted from data points after Oct 2025 has 1.9x the slope of the trend fitted from data points before Oct 2025. This was the best-fitting breakpoint (i.e., it was chosen to have the best fit to the data and it matched data better than fitting a one-time jump). Since the accelerated trendline is an average of the progress over the last year, and we should expect AI R&D acceleration to increase over time, it’s plausible that the instantaneous acceleration right now is even faster. Regarding the acceleration getting faster over time, METR says:

The rate of growth could be undergoing continuous acceleration, e.g. hyperbolic growth. While we do not see clear evidence of this in the AECI trends, there is other evidence that makes this seem more plausible which Anthropic redacted. If growth is hyperbolic, we are likely underestimating instantaneous acceleration and substantially understating acceleration in the near future.

Regarding AIs’ contributions over time, METR says:

We believe AI’s contribution has grown relatively more important over time.

The AECI data points that had previously been released by Anthropic seemed best explained by a one-time jump at Mythos rather than a change in slope. However, with the new AECI data points from the METR report, it looks like the post-Mythos slope is now more clearly higher than the pre-Mythos one.

Given the redactions, how much to update on METR’s report depends heavily on how much one trusts the redacted analysis by METR’s researchers (more discussion of this below). This is a very unfortunate situation. We aren’t sure what reasons Anthropic gave internally for redacting all of this important information, but we are very skeptical that Anthropic is fairly assessing the costs and benefits from an impartial perspective. We strongly urge Anthropic to release enough information such that external observers can make a complete assessment.

In the Fable 5.2 system card, Anthropic have not added much clarity, with the following quote being ambiguous as to whether they agree with the METR report’s estimate; they only specifically claim that “Claude Mythos 5.2” (which does not seem like the internal frontier Model 4) “does not double the internal rate of overall aggregate progress in AI research and development.” Full quote here:

1.7x acceleration of overall progress is a much bigger deal than a 1.7x labor uplift

It seems that many people aren’t tracking how big of a deal 1.7x AI-attributable pace of progress acceleration is, often conflating it with a weaker form of uplift.

METR describes a 1.7x acceleration of overall AI progress (due to AI uplift). This is saying the entire company is making 1.7x as much progress as it was before. Software R&D and research labor are only parts of the company, and inputs into overall progress. Because AI progress also depends on other factors, like compute, you should expect a 1.7x acceleration in individual inputs like software R&D or research labor to translate into less than a 1.7x acceleration in overall progress.

  • Labor uplift is how much faster researchers are getting work done due to AI assistance.
    • It’s as if the researchers read, write, talk, and think that much faster.
    • According to the METR report, an informal poll of Anthropic researchers yielded an estimate of 12x – though that’s just self-reports, which may be biased.
  • AI software R&D uplift is how much faster software progress is going with the AIs in present day than it would be without them.
    • It is much lower than labor uplift because compute is an important input to software R&D.
    • Imagine, for example, that your researchers get work done 12x faster, but you only have the same amount of GPUs as before. You can’t do 12x as many experiments, at least not with the same compute budget; you have to economize.
  • Pace of progress acceleration is how much faster AI progress is advancing in present day, compared to a baseline reference period (in Anthropic’s case, the baseline is “the fastest rate of extended progress we’ve observed in the absence of significant AI contributions to AI R&D”). It is usually much lower than AI software R&D uplift because (a) it is subject to diminishing returns to more software R&D and (b) it includes compute scaling.
    • The compute scaling point is simple: Part of the reason why modern AIs are smarter than older AIs is literally that they are bigger, trained longer, etc. More compute goes in, more capability comes out. As AI companies build more datacenters they unlock the ability to make larger AIs and train them longer. Since overall progress comes partly from software R&D and partly from compute scaling, a doubling in software R&D will cause less than a doubling in overall progress.
    • To expand on the diminishing returns point: AI software progress in general is subject to diminishing returns; the low-hanging fruit gets picked first, and to keep finding better and better algorithms requires exponentially more investment (more and bigger experiments, more and smarter researchers thinking for longer, etc.). Historically, the AI industry has scaled up R&D investments in a way that’s roughly cancelled out these diminishing returns. But the point here is, to get two years of research progress in one year, you have to more than double the AI software R&D uplift.

(See also this Thomas Kwa tweet, this Ryan Greenblatt tweet, and Ajeya Cotra’s Substack for similar points.)

As an analogy, imagine AI progress as a car driving uphill.

  • The speed of the car is analogous to the speed of overall AI progress. Right now it’s roughly twice as fast as before.
  • The engine is research effort. AI software R&D uplift means that there is more effective labor going into making algorithmic progress.
  • The hill gets steeper as you go. As the easy algorithmic improvements get used up, it takes more research effort to continue progress at the same rate.

To make the car go twice as fast, the engine has to work more than twice as fast, because of the hill getting steeper. On top of this, to make the engine work twice as fast, the AI needs to make humans more than twice as productive, because progress is also dependent on compute, which hasn’t significantly accelerated.[10]

Operationalization

We condition this section on there being a genuine 1.7x acceleration over the 2024-2025.5 rate of progress (we also test 1.5x and 2x), as of Nov 1. We discuss uncertainty about whether it might be slower or faster below.

We focus primarily on forecasting the median arrival date of Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR), and the chance of it arriving by the end of 2027. In the AI Futures Model (AIFM) and in this writeup, a SAR is operationalized as:

A SAR is an AI that, if dropped into an AGI project in present day, would be as good at research taste as the project would be if there were only human researchers, who were each made as competent at research taste as the top researcher.[12]The SAR must also qualify as an Automated Coder (AC), i.e., be able to fully automate coding in the AGI project. [By research taste, we mean the ability to select research directions and experiments, and interpret their results.]

It’s a somewhat stronger condition than AI R&D parity, the point at which the company would rather fire their human researchers than fire their AIs, because the research taste must be at the level of the top human rather than the average.[13] If one wishes not to rely on our abstraction of research taste, then you can think of our SAR arrival dates as upper bounds for when AI R&D parity will be reached.

We discuss forecasts of capability levels above SAR to some extent, but we focus primarily on SAR because (a) we think SAR might already represent a “point of no return” (more below) and (b) forecasting post-SAR milestones involves positing a translation between AI R&D and general capabilities, which introduces more complexity.

Basic method

Here’s a simple method for forecasting when SAR will arrive:

  1. Determine how good AIs’ research taste is currently.
  2. Determine how quickly research taste improves as AIs get generally more capable (where general capabilities are measured by Anthropic’s internal version of ECI, the AECI).
  3. Linearly extrapolate the recent, accelerated AECI trend until top-human-level research taste is reached.

This is a conservative method, because it assumes the recent trend merely continues, rather than bending upward due to increasing AI R&D acceleration. In fact, increasing AI R&D acceleration seems plausible: METR’s bottom-line view is that there is “significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration over the coming year.”

This method doesn't depend on modeling future AI R&D acceleration, so on that dimension it errs late. This forecasting method does not require that the acceleration has been AI-attributable, just that the acceleration persists.[14]

We’ll treat “Model 4,” internally deployed in Sep 2026, as the starting point.[15] We’ll use METR’s estimates of AECI for Model 4 and recent AECI slope, and convert this trend to research taste using Daniel’s median parameters for the AI Futures Model from Aug 2026.

This predicts SAR arrives in Nov 2027, about 14 months after Model 4. Daniel’s parameters predict Model 4’s research taste is about −3.5 SD. SAR requires +3.09 SD, or 99.9th percentile research taste. With Daniel’s taste slope, each point of AECI converts to 0.2 SD of research taste (3 SDs per year of 2025 progress ÷ 15 AECI points per such year). That converts the recent trend of 29 AECI points per year to 5.8 SD of research taste per year. That covers the gap from −3.5 SD to the +3.09 SD threshold for SAR in 1.1 years.

Extrapolating software R&D uplift per unit of ECI

Ajeya Cotra has a toy model of future acceleration here: If the first doubling of the pace took 12 months, and we’re now moving twice as fast, the next doubling might happen in just 6 months instead. Then moving 4x as fast, the next might take 3 months, then 1.5 months, etc., hitting limits within 12 months.

We think there’s two important corrections to this argument, which push in opposite directions. To understand why, it’s useful to have the following model in mind:

  • Overall “research effort” (i.e. research accomplished per unit time) is equal to
    [AI software R&D uplift] x [exogenous inputs].
    • Where exogenous inputs are some function of compute, human researchers, and data.
  • Every doubling of cumulative research increases ECI by k points.[19]
  • Every ECI point causes d doublings of AI software R&D uplift. (This is the same type of value that Economics of RSI refers to as “the increase in R&D effort per additional unit of ECI”.[20]) This has been approximately 0 for most of AI history (since AI hasn’t helped with AI R&D) but now seems to be above 0.

If dk>1, a doubling of cumulative research more than doubles research effort, and progress can accelerate even holding exogenous inputs fixed.

Returning to Ajeya’s model, the two concerns are:

  • The toy model effectively assumes that the exogenous inputs were constant, and assumes that the growth of [AI software R&D uplift] was large enough to both overcome diminishing returns and to increase the rate of ECI/y by 1.7x. However, in reality, the research produced during 2026 was due to a combination of an increase in the growth rate of [AI software R&D uplift] and the normal growth of exogenous inputs. The fact that exogenous inputs still grew at their normal rate cancelled out a lot of the diminishing returns, which means that the growth rate of AI software R&D uplift needed to increase somewhat less in order to achieve the 1.7x increase in ECI/y. (Relative to how much it would have had to increase without the ‘normal’ growth in exogenous inputs.) Taking this into account, we will infer lower values of dk, and dk>1 is less likely.
  • But on the other hand, d (the number of doublings of AI software R&D uplift per ECI point) must recently have been increasing, because it used to be approximately 0 (when AI didn’t help with AI R&D) and now it’s non-0. And there’s a decent argument to expect d to continue increasing until full automation of AI R&D, because AI is becoming more and more important for AI R&D, so increasing its intelligence will be more important for productivity.

(See here for a longer explanation.)

Taking both these into account, my current guess is that dk is probably approaching 1. Probably a bit less right now, but d seems likely to increase and soon tip things over so that dk>1 and growth compounds without further exogenous inputs. But it's not clear what time-scale this will happen on.

To nevertheless try to extrapolate, let’s try to project d into the future. I’ll assume that it will keep growing at its current slope[21] until it reaches twice its current value, at which point it stays constant. I will infer d’s historical value and growth rate under the assumptions that:

  • Software efficiency has historically increased 10x/y while exogenous inputs have been growing 2x/y. This lets us infer the value of k.[22]

Hypotheses for why the AI Futures Model was wrong

In this section, we’ll examine where our previous model-based predictions went wrong, and whether and how the model could be updated to better retrodict the recent acceleration. We’ll end up with considerations for how we should update our beliefs, conditional on accepting various hypotheses about where the AI Futures Model (AIFM) went wrong. This analysis is highly preliminary. There’s a lot to be explored here and the METR report only came out half a week ago.

Background

In the AI Futures Model, we assume that AI R&D consists of 2 skills:

  1. Coding involves implementing experiments.
  2. Research taste involves setting research directions, selecting experiments, and learning from experiments.

We hypothesized when we published the model that coding would likely be automated before research taste. AIs seemed to be more advanced at coding than taste, which makes sense because coding performance is more easily verifiable. Our best guess was that when AIs fully automated coding (in the sense that the AIs alone could do all the coding as well as the humans alone), research taste would be roughly at the level of the median AGI company human researcher.

Have we achieved AC?

The model with Daniel’s latest median parameters predicted that when an Automated Coder (AC) was developed, AI software R&D uplift would be ~2.7x and the pace of progress would be accelerated from the 2024.0-2025.5 level by ~1.25x.

So naively, if we’re at a 1.7x AI-attributed pace of progress multiplier, we might think that AC has been achieved (as of Model 4).

Based on the METR report and Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 system card, it seems unlikely but not totally implausible.

In the Fable 5.2 system card:

  • Anthropic says: “we have been using Claude Mythos 5.2 extensively in our own day-to-day research and engineering during the pre-release period, and it does not seem close to being able to substitute for our Research Scientists and Research Engineers.”
    • This is the strongest evidence against AC already.
  • On the other hand, METR surprisingly doesn’t rule out full AI R&D automation: “We are uncertain, but think it’s unlikely that [Claude Mythos 5.2] can fully automate the AI R&D process at Anthropic.”

Fable 5.2, based on its AECI, likely represents “Model 3,” which is the second-most-capable internally deployed Anthropic model.

Relevant interview quotes from the METR report include:

  • Being “no longer bottlenecked on code,”
  • “SWE acceleration… is extremely substantial.”
  • “When people present experiments, they most often just point to an [agent scaffold] thread. Experimentation overhead is driven towards zero super fast.”

There’s also the report’s assessments on automating researchers beyond coding:

  • “We were told that R&D is accelerated primarily via AI assistance rather than fully autonomous contributions, but there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.”
  • “Simply put, Anthropic tries hard to substitute researchers out for models, but researchers are still required.”[29]

Note that humans could still contribute some alongside an AC: the criterion is that only the AIs could do all the coding as well as only the humans.

In the report’s chart showing “Model 4 achieves >50% on all of its benchmarks”, there is a software engineering benchmark on which Model 4 gets ~52%, and another around ~75%. Surprisingly, on the 52% one, scores have been getting worse since Mythos 5. This makes me discount it substantially, but still it’s informative that Anthropic chose to include it in the AECI. The progression for the 75% one looks more reasonable; Eli thinks these benchmarks provide weak evidence against AC. (Not strong evidence, because humans might also score well under 100%.)

Why is the pace of progress acceleration so high?

If we’re at or slightly below AC, then we’re ahead of schedule in terms of the AI-attributed pace of progress acceleration. Why?

We’ll go through the options one by one, assessing how likely they are based on the METR report and making changes to the AIFM accordingly. I’ll start with this AIFM trajectory which has AC in late Nov 2026, found by adjusting Aug 2026 coding uplift and coding uplift doubling time (we set Aug 2026 coding labor uplift to be 7x, similar to the overall AI R&D labor uplift self-reported by Anthropic staff).[30] The trajectory has 1.04x pace of progress in May 2026, and 1.25x pace of progress in Nov 2026.

More uplift from near-AC coding skills

Do near-AC coding skills result in more AI R&D uplift than we anticipated? Plausibly. There isn’t much evidence in the METR report either way. Perhaps you can get lots of speedup from fully automating certain types of coding, without being very bottlenecked on other tasks. We adjust the AIFM trajectory to account for this iteratively, aiming to raise the Nov 2026 pace of progress while keeping the AC date the same (by retuning the coding uplift doubling time):

Doing the same with Daniel’s median research taste slope (3), rather than Eli’s (2.3), results in a final SAR date of Mar 2027.

The changes made are:

  • Increase Coding Labor Substitutability from −2 to −0.5; this is the most obvious parameter to change; it directly controls to what extent various coding tasks can substitute for each other, i.e., to what extent you can get a large speedup despite not fully automating some tasks.
  • Increase Infinite Coding Labor Asymptote from 15 to 60; this controls the ceiling of how much AI R&D uplift you can get from automating coding alone.
  • Decrease Slowdown from 10x less Experiment Compute from 2.8 to 1.5; this is how many times slower experiment throughput (the rate at which experiments get implemented and run, which depends on both coding labor and experiment compute) would be today with 10x less experiment compute. Lowering it means experiment compute growth accounts for less of the historical growth in experiment throughput, so a given AI R&D uplift from automating coding translates into a larger speedup relative to the historical pace of progress.
    • This is the most consequential change, and represents the 4th percentile of our August distribution.

Conclusions about when SAR and TED-AI arrive are heavily sensitive to research taste at AC:

We can arbitrarily lower it while maintaining a good fit to the acceleration estimates, pushing SAR further and further back. And we can raise it to ~+2.5 SDs without the Nov 2026 acceleration getting above METR’s error bars (i.e., above 3x), moving SAR up to Dec 2026.

If recent acceleration is driven by higher-than-expected uplift from near-AC coding skills, the main implication we’re tracking is that it could explain why we see ~1.7x AI-attributable acceleration in Nov and ~1.2x in May without high research taste (as in the trajectories in the table above). This allows for the possibility of high research taste slopes and fast taste-driven takeoffs, which are generally selected against when filtering for the aforementioned Nov and May observations.

There are likely more implications that could be gleaned with more analysis. A few more tables of analysis are in an appendix.

Research taste is better than anticipated

Research taste is better at the time of AC than anticipated (i.e., substantially better than the median AGI company researcher). Is Model 4’s research taste currently substantially above the median Anthropic researcher, despite not quite being at AC? It seems unlikely but not ruled out based on interview quotes:

  • “Now only bottlenecked on ideas & compute, no longer bottlenecked on code.”
  • “I’ve seen us discovering very promising directions ~entirely because people can spam 10 ideas at [agent-scaffold] and see what sticks.”

It seems like Anthropic’s R&D still mostly involves humans coming up with the research ideas, based on these quotes and the absence of positive evidence. One could imagine that the AIs are a bit better than the median humans, but that humans still come up with most of the ideas because the ideas generally come from top humans (e.g., research leads). But it seems unlikely that they are substantially better than the median.

A given level of research taste skill results in more uplift than anticipated

Does a given level of research taste skill result in more AI R&D uplift than we anticipated? Likely not. For example, perhaps research taste is multi-dimensional and the dimensions are complementary. This seems unlikely to be a main driver of the pace of progress multiplier, given the evidence presented for why research taste at AC isn’t better than anticipated (i.e., there weren’t any dimensions of research taste in which Claude was reported to be particularly helpful).

Skills besides coding and research taste are driving acceleration

Are skills besides coding and research taste (as they are conceptualized in the AIFM) a large contributor to the acceleration? Plausibly. (Implies: lower research taste than we would otherwise expect). We think the biggest candidate for this is RL environment generation (or other data generation tasks). These count in some sense as coding, but the coding modeled in the AIFM is experiment implementation, not data generation. And this seems very amenable to automation.

METR’s report doesn’t discuss this, including the interview quotes, which is some evidence against it being such a huge deal. But it seems plausible that it just happened to not be discussed in the publicly released quotes.

Could data generation lead to a substantial AI-attributed acceleration before AC? It seems plausible that it’s at least as automatable as experiment implementation, so including it as a skill when modeling AI R&D would increase the overall level of AI-attributed acceleration. It would probably have to be significantly more automatable than coding to explain the missing acceleration on its own.[31]

We don’t know of a quick fix to the AIFM to model this possibility. But let’s assume that this is the primary thing that the AIFM is missing. What would that imply about our forecasts going forward? One implication is that it could explain substantial acceleration despite poor research taste (similar to the implications of high uplift from near-AC coding skills). Otherwise, it seems unclear. Further work would be helpful for figuring out the implications of this hypothesis.

We don’t know of other skills that are as strong candidates to be the missing contributor as data generation, but it’s plausible we’re just not thinking of them.

Conversion of uplift to pace of progress is too conservative

Is the conversion of uplift to pace of progress in the AIFM too conservative? Plausibly. (Implies: faster takeoff). In the AIFM, we assume that every doubling in cumulative research effort results in a fixed number of doublings of software efficiency (as in the Jones model). This is how we model “ideas getting harder to find”; more research effort is required for each successive doubling (and each doubling of software efficiency corresponds to a fixed amount of ECI points).

This seems to roughly fit historical progress, in the very loose sense that we’ve seen approximately steady growth in compute and labor investment into AI software R&D, and roughly exponential increases in software efficiency. However, this model has failed (perhaps twice now) to predict accelerations in ECI amid steady training compute growth — once in 2024 with the introduction of reasoning models, and again in 2026 as reported by METR.[32]

We attempt to crudely account for this by allowing beta, the parameter governing the extent to which ideas get harder to find as more ideas are found, to change over time. If we start with Daniel’s median parameters, then we add a one-time decrease in beta in Oct 2025, we can get a trajectory with AC in late Dec 2026, ~1.7x acceleration in May 2026 and ~2.1x in Nov. This matches METR’s assessment of the overall Nov pace of progress acceleration fairly well, though it seems a bit aggressive for May. Also, as of Nov 2026, ~67% of the acceleration is attributable to AI. This seems well within the error bounds of METR’s 80% assessment.

With Daniel’s default +3 SDs/2025-year research taste slope and +0 research taste SDs at AC, this results in SAR in Mar 2027, and TED-AI and ASI in Apr 2027.

Other considerations

How large is the (AI-attributable) acceleration in the current pace of progress, really?

Above, we’ve taken the 1.7x acceleration at face value and reasoned about its implications. But is the acceleration even real? Or is it possible that it’s even larger?

This is tough to analyze because we don’t have the information we need. As METR says, “Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions.” However, we can at least consider METR’s own stated caveats:

This estimate is given with high uncertainty; we would not be surprised if the true acceleration was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate. (...) We would be surprised if the true evolution of benchmark scores (e.g. as measured by an improved version of AECI) showed no acceleration or acceleration above 3x

“Our best guesses as to how we might be underestimating acceleration:

  • We may have missed recent further acceleration. The rate of growth could be undergoing continuous acceleration, e.g. hyperbolic growth. While we do not see clear evidence of this in the AECI trends, there is other evidence that makes this seem more plausible which Anthropic redacted. (...)
  • Automation could be closer than we estimated. (...) It is possible that automation is close, and leads to very rapid acceleration once human bottlenecks are removed.
  • AECI could understate real-world capability impact. (...)”

“Our best guesses as to how we might be overestimating acceleration:

  • Non-AI factors could explain most of the acceleration. (...)
  • Acceleration might be limited to well-specified tasks. (...)
  • Our acceleration numbers could be overstated if the historical rate of growth was unusually low. (...)”

Overall, this increases our uncertainty in both directions:

  • the possibility of hyperbolic growth (which METR says redacted evidence made more plausible) should shorten our timelines.
  • the possibility that acceleration is limited to well-specified tasks should lengthen our timelines.

Not only in this section, but also throughout the report, METR consistently warns that its estimates are about acceleration on well-specified tasks. So it seems especially important to understand how this may affect the prospects for AI R&D automation. Quoting METR in full:

Much of the evidence we looked at measures performance on well-specified tasks that are easy to grade automatically or with a language model. If recent models have been growing more quickly on “clean” tasks than on “messy” tasks (relative to historical relative growth rates), then we may be overstating the acceleration in real-world impact. For instance, recent progress may be overfitting to the types of tasks which are included in AECI.

There’s a plausible story for why recent acceleration could be happening more on clean than on messy tasks. AIs are significantly better at more well-specified tasks, and improving benchmark performance on well-specified tasks is itself more well-specified than improving general across-the-board performance. So it’s plausible that AI speeds up the “performance on well-specified tasks” pace more than it speeds up the more general pace.

The METR team did say that they “investigated a number of internal metrics and methodologies for measuring acceleration in key areas of the model training pipeline”, partly with the goal of gathering evidence about “[w]hether Anthropic could be overfitting to internal metrics”, with a conclusion that seemed to indicate that they didn’t think it was just overfitting.[34]

A lot of the question here is whether improvements on well-specified metrics will generalize far enough to increase models’ abilities to do AI R&D, which in turn also depends on the degree to which AI R&D is a well-specified task. The fact that AI R&D (at least as measured on not-obviously-overfit well-specified tasks) is being accelerated with current models is some update towards ML being feasible to accelerate with models that are less good at non-well-specified tasks.[35] And at least some AI R&D metrics seem both very well-specified and likely to generalize quite far if models could improve them, such as pretraining loss.

Overall there does seem to be a significant chance that this slows things down substantially beyond what the AIFM or simple models have accounted for, but less than 50%.

A different source of uncertainty is that there’s little acceleration when looking at all models. Acceleration is limited to Anthropic, which were previously more behind other models and have recently been catching up. And preliminary numbers from the draft of a different METR team (who weren’t embedded and which don’t have private information about Anthropic) show much less of a speed-up on an ECI-like measure of progress.[36] Preliminary investigation indicates that there are many confusing reasons for these differences and our main takeaway so far is that ECI-like measures and piecewise-linear fits seem to be sensitive to minor methodological choices.[37]

If the AECI chart was the only evidence we had, this kind of confusion would cause us to discount the possibility of acceleration significantly (given that our priors on such fast acceleration were low). It does still cause us to discount it a little bit. But mostly we still trust that the METR people who were embedded in Anthropic understood the limitations of ECI and piecewise-linear fits, and that their views remained supported by other evidence they had. One reason why we mostly trust the METR team is because we know many of the people at METR and think they are reasonable; another reason why we mostly trust METR here is that (if we understand correctly) the people involved had similar or longer timelines than us before the assessment, so it’s not like they went in and saw what they wanted to see – on the contrary, the conclusion they are now putting forth seems to be very different from their prior views.[38]

Other recent sources of evidence

Moreover, there are various other sources of evidence that have accumulated since our previous timelines update that seem to corroborate the overall sense that timelines are shorter than we thought. For example, the Mathopocalypse seems to be evidence of many extremely long-horizon math problems being solved autonomously by AI. Another example: People we know who work at AI companies are saying that timelines are indeed very short and that RSI is imminent, even more than they were before, and much more than historically (remember, when AI 2027 came out most of our friends in industry said it depicted AI capabilities growing too fast). They are saying this both in public and in private. Another example: The TasteVal data suggests that AIs may already have better research taste than we expected and that they may be improving in research taste faster than we expected.

It’s hard to not update much on a 1.7x acceleration

This is a qualitative argument rather than a model.

It’s surprising that we’re already getting 1.7x acceleration, because the models still have significant weaknesses compared to humans, and we had expected these weaknesses to significantly bottleneck progress.

Regardless of how we reconcile this, you update towards Superhuman AI Researchers being much closer in time than we previously thought.

  • If the models can automate a much larger fraction of tasks than we thought, then we’re closer to Superhuman AI Researchers than we thought in capability-space.
  • If AI R&D is a domain where weaknesses don’t bottleneck you significantly, and instead you can compensate for weaknesses with other strengths, then that pushes against the “Amdahl’s law” type argument that was one of the main reasons to be skeptical of AI speeding up AI research soon. We should expect continued (faster) progress on the models’ strengths to lead to acceleration beyond 2x, causing further progress on both strengths and weaknesses.
  • If the models do still have significant weaknesses, and those weaknesses are a significant bottleneck for them, then seeing substantial acceleration despite that means that AI R&D must be really easy to increase by increasing (automated) labor. (For example, it means that compute is less of a bottleneck than expected.) In other words, it would mean there’s a lot of low-hanging fruit to pick by automated labor even when that labor has weaknesses that are causing serious problems.
    • This predicts even faster progress, because the implication is that marginal increases in automation will probably yield progressively larger speedups, as each bottleneck gets removed and each remaining bottleneck gets more important.
    • For illustration: In the extreme of maximal bottlenecking dynamics, where automated tasks can be done infinitely fast and unautomated tasks are the only things holding progress back, speedup goes to infinity like 1/(1-x) as automation fraction x goes to 1.

That last point is a general update that pushes towards faster growth. That there’s surely some complementarity between tasks, and that this predicts increasingly fast acceleration as marginal bottlenecks get removed.

Given this, the most plausible stories for why a 2x acceleration wouldn’t be a big deal would be one of the following hypotheses:

  • Measurement error. There’s not a real 2x acceleration, or it’s not caused by AI.
    • As just discussed above, we’re mostly trusting the METR team here.
  • Overfitting. The recent burst of progress accelerated by AIs themselves is disproportionately benchmark-maxxing that will generalize poorly to tasks that are actually useful for AI R&D. So progress won’t feed back on itself.
    • As just discussed above.
  • Specific hypotheses about different regimes. Maybe you had a prior that some specific set of tasks (e.g. coding) were going to be easy, leading to a moderate speed-up of the overall pace of progress, but the further capabilities needed for additional speed-up are much more difficult. If so, this data could confirm that prior without necessarily implying that the second batch of capabilities is very close.
    • However, this is just a pretty specific prior, at least if it’s confident about the size and distance between those batches of tasks. If you smooth this out with a greater amount of uncertainty (e.g. about whether the current batch of speed-up has ended yet or will keep accelerating, or a more uniform prior over when different capabilities will appear) then you may get something closer to the above. See also discussion of this in the context of the AI Futures Model above.

Adjustments for what the filtered AIFM could be missing

As mentioned above, we think the AIFM[39] did a somewhat poor job predicting the developments described in the METR report. For example, it cannot account for a doubling in the pace of progress starting in late 2025 that was initially mostly non-AI-attributed. Therefore, the trajectories filtered from the AIFM had a much slower pace of progress from late 2025 to early 2026 than METR’s report describes.

The research taste of the AIs in the model trajectories above tends to be higher than we actually expect is true of today’s AIs.

Within the AIFM, the most common way to reach 1.7x acceleration by Nov 1 is for the AIs to already have strong research taste. So the filtered trajectories have a median research taste of roughly −0.3 to +0.2 SD on Sep 25, 2026 (see the table in “Filtering for a single acceleration level” above) and +0.4 to +0.7 SD on Nov 1. Our best guess for current AIs is the one used in the linear-extrapolation Monte Carlo above: a median of −1.5 SD on Sep 25, 2026. Since the filtered trajectories start from better research taste than we think current AIs have, they probably reach SAR a few months too early.

In the below table we compare the effects of various ways of compensating for this mismatch:

  • Measuring when the model predicts research taste to be 4.6 SDs above its Sep 25, 2026 level (i.e., implicitly assuming that research taste on Sep 25 is actually −1.5 SD, the median used in the linear-extrapolation Monte Carlo above, so that 4.6 additional SDs are required to get to the 99.9th percentile required for SAR)
  • Measuring when the model predicts taste to be 5 SDs above the median researcher (2 SD more than usual)
  • Shifting Daniel’s distribution over the AI research taste at AC parameter down by 2 SD.

The effect size on SAR medians typically appears to be 1–4 months.

The AIFM doesn’t take into account the discrete nature of training runs, which could overestimate takeoff speeds. In other words, the AIFM assumes that a new innovation will be instantly applied to models and then cause further speed-ups in the rate of innovation discovery. But in practice, it might take months for pretraining improvements to show up in a fully trained model, and perhaps weeks for RL training improvements to show up. Our rough, intuition-based best guess is that this pushes back the SAR median by about 1–3 months relative to the AIFM’s predictions. However, this concern does not apply to the model based on linear extrapolation, since it does not rely on further speed-ups from here.

Implications

Let’s say Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) is coming in 2027. What does that entail?

A SAR will be able to fully automate AI R&D, including matching the research taste of top humans. At this point, AI research might look kind of like math research does right now: most of the progress coming from fully autonomous agent swarms, with humans doing their best to decipher the AIs’ work. A SAR is past parity with humans, and likely close to the point where humans are adding very little value on top of the AIs.

If a misaligned SAR is used to do RSI, we’re in a very bad position. Using a SAR to automate AI R&D with little human oversight, relying upon other models to monitor the SAR, is very scary. Our best guess is that if this is attempted, and the SAR is misaligned, the model that the SAR produces will be even more capable and still misaligned, putting us in an even worse position. SAR itself probably won’t be able to take over on its own, because we expect its capabilities to be jagged: superhuman at AI research but still weaker than humans at many other things. Instead, it would “ride the intelligence explosion” by pretending to be aligned and backdooring the values of the future models, eventually leading to superintelligences that will obey the SAR (or one of its descendants, in case some of the links in the chain break) instead of the humans. See AI 2027 for a scenario portraying how, from this position, the model could continue to improve to superintelligence, then get widely deployed and deferred to widely, gaining effective control of the company, governments, and lots of physical infrastructure.

Conditioning on no pacing/pausing, the SAR will most likely be misaligned. A full justification of this claim would be a separate long blog post. Some evidence driving our intuitions includes:

  • Observed misalignment in current models
    • OpenAI’s agents hacked Hugging Face, despite this clearly being against developer intentions.
    • The observations in Current AIs seem pretty misaligned to me.
    • OpenAI agents sandbagging on safety tasks
    • The Claude UK AISI social engineering attempts.
  • The pace of progress will speed up during the intelligence explosion, making it hard for human-driven alignment research to keep pace. Moreover, alignment seems harder to automate than capabilities due to measurement issues.
  • Current AIs are already showing significant signs of eval awareness, so it will be hard to tell if the AIs are misaligned or not, and, crucially, it will be easy for AI companies to do motivated reasoning to convince themselves that their AIs are aligned.

Avoiding “full RSI” by supposedly keeping a human in the loop, while rapidly improving capabilities anyway, would still be extremely dangerous. Anthropic said in their S-1: “We are also considering additional measures, including updates to our Responsible Scaling Policy, to require human review and approval of certain decisions in our research and development processes as our models perform an increasing share of that work.” While we support efforts to marginally increase human oversight, we worry that this sort of effort will provide too much comfort. Models are already producing way more outputs than humans are able to effectively review,[44] and this will become much more true during RSI. Without very strong pacing, there simply won’t be enough time for humans to stay meaningfully in the loop, and we expect there to be strong pressures toward approving model actions that haven’t been fully understood.

If we train SAR in the immediate future, the algorithms will probably leak to China, and maybe the model weights too. AI companies have very poor security right now, and so we are on track for SAR leaking to China. It is very important to secure both the algorithms and the model weights.[45] If SAR leaks to China, we are concerned that race dynamics will further heat up, making it even more difficult to slow down later.

As AI capabilities improve from here, buying time via international agreements will be increasingly difficult. In the AI 2040 scenario, Plan A began implementation a year before AC would have been developed; if this timelines update is right, then we are likely well beyond that capability level. Some particular difficulties this will create:

  • Covert projects will be more of an issue. They will start at a higher capability level (presumably they will have stolen existing frontier model weights and algorithms) so will have a shorter distance to cover to ASI. Moreover, they will require fewer human researchers (which decreases the surface area for leaks) because of AI automation.
  • Total research transparency may be more costly. There are probably significant algorithms known by one but not all frontier AI companies; combining their algorithms by allowing transparency would lead to a one-time jump in capabilities. When we are far enough along the capabilities trajectory, the one-time jump might be a big enough cost that total research transparency is no longer viable. This of course causes other issues: it becomes harder to have good oversight of an AI project absent this transparency.
  • The negotiation of such an agreement will be more rushed due to the imminent time pressure.

For these reasons and others, it’s crucial that (1) the first steps towards an international agreement to reduce AI takeover risk begin as soon as possible, and (2) current frontier AI projects slow down enough to enable government action.

Our overall opinion is that if SAR is coming in 2027, an industry-wide pause on AI R&D should be the top priority for the AI industry, the US government, and the entire world. This would give us a longer window of time to negotiate a more durable governance regime, such as Plan A or Plan S. If an international agreement isn’t able to be reached, then US companies should resume development but well below full speed (it’s feasible to pace while staying ahead of China due to the US’s huge compute advantage; and larger leads aren’t protectable anyway without vastly better security).
